title: Can AI predict machine failures before they stop your line?
description: When predictive maintenance software pays, when your PM program is enough, and what a 10-machine start costs: 14 offerings priced 26 Nov 2026.
verdict: Scheduled overhauls miss most failures. In airline and navy studies, most failures were random, not age-based.[^1][^2]
Predictive saves 8-12% over preventive, per DOE, but false alarms can wipe that out.[^3][^4]
Clean your work orders first. Entry errors skew maintenance KPIs, and most records skip how a fault was found.[^5][^6]
Self-run sensors for 10 machines list at about $4,200 to $5,550 in hardware, per our 26 Nov check.[^7][^8]
People still make the call. ISO 17359 leaves inspect, slow down or stop to your team.[^9][^10]

summary: Predictive maintenance software reads machine data, like vibration and temperature, plus work-order history, and flags machines starting to fail.[^3][^11] What AI changes: it spots fault trends early, so planners book repairs before breakdowns; DOE puts predictive at 8-12% cheaper than scheduled maintenance.[^11][^3] False alarms decide whether it pays.[^4]
humanRole: Technician: confirms each alert on the machine, with a handheld reading or a look and listen, before parts are ordered. Inspection is one of the calls ISO 17359 lists after an alert.[^9][^10]
Maintenance planner: decides when the repair happens, around production. The standard's options run from keep monitoring to bring maintenance forward or stop the machine.[^10]
Maintenance manager: picks which machines are watched, sets alarm levels and signs off run-or-stop calls. Time to failure still needs expert judgment, per NIST's summary of ISO 13381-1.[^13]
Electrical gear stays with qualified people: NFPA 70B wants corrective action decided and recorded by them. OSHA lockout rules still cover every repair an alert triggers.[^14][^15]
teamAfter: From firefighting to planned work: an alert gives lead time, so the planner books the job before the breakdown does. In MaintainX's vendor survey, half of teams spend under 40% of their time on planned work.[^16]
From tribal knowledge to written work orders: 74% of teams have a critical asset only one person can repair, per Limble's vendor survey. Better notes feed the model and keep that know-how.[^17][^18]
Technicians make the model better. In McKinsey's offshore case, maintenance teams and data scientists removed false alarms failure by failure.[^19][^20]
Jobs grow: BLS projects maintenance mechanic jobs up 14% to 2035. Among AI-using firms, 66% only use it to help staff; 2% saw AI-related employment fall.[^21][^22]

example.input: Illustrative. A wireless vibration and temperature sensor on a critical cooling-water pump with no spare, reading every few minutes for 3 months. Plus 18 months of the pump's free-text work orders ("brg noisy", "greased", "replaced coupling insert") and its run hours.[^18]
example.output: Flag: Pump P-12 outboard bearing vibration has risen for 3 weeks, temperature normal, matching two past bearing work orders. Next step: a technician confirms with a handheld reading this week; if confirmed, the planner books the swap for Saturday changeover.[^10] Confidence: medium, after one false alarm in August; stores hold the bearing but not the insert.[^4]

tables.title: Predictive or preventive maintenance: which fits each machine?
tables.intro: In airline and navy studies, most failures were random, so calendar work alone can't prevent them.[^1][^23] Those figures come from aircraft and ships, not plant averages, so treat them as a guide.[^24]

rows.name: Wears out with use and has a clear life (belts, filters, brushes)
cells: Time- or usage-based preventive maintenance (PM)[^23]
Age-related failures were 8-23% in the studies NASA cites; calendar PM does catch these.[^1][^23]

rows.name: Fails at random but gives warning (bearings, gearboxes, motors, pumps)
cells: Condition checks, then predictive[^23]
Random failures were 77-92% in the same studies; a warning period lets a check catch them.[^1][^23]

rows.name: Cheap, redundant and quick to swap
cells: Run to failure, by choice[^3]
Monitoring would cost more than the failure.[^3][^2]

rows.name: Critical, with known failure modes, or many identical units
cells: AI prediction worth a trial[^12]
This is where McKinsey finds advanced prediction pays; for one narrow failure mode, simple thresholds often do.[^12][^19]

rows.name: Electrical gear (switchgear, panels, motor control centers)
cells: Scheduled infrared scans under an NFPA 70B program[^14]
NFPA 70B sets scans every 12 months for gear in good condition, every 6 months in poor condition (Condition 3).[^25][^26]

recipes.name: 1. No sensors yet: start from your work orders
recipes.when: PM completion is shaky, the CMMS (maintenance software) is half-used, or there's no hardware budget. Deloitte says get the basics in place first; in Limble's vendor survey, 39% of teams use their CMMS consistently.[^29][^17]
flow: Maintenance planner: export 2-3 years of work orders to a spreadsheet
Reliability lead: tag them with NIST's free Nestor tool, or an AI chatbot checked by hand, to find repeat failures by asset[^31][^18]
Maintenance manager: rank assets by criticality and repeat failures, and pick the top 10 within a month
Planner: review each PM task on those assets; keep it if the wear is age-related, else switch it to an inspection[^1][^23]
Technician: add a "how was this found" field to every new work order[^6]
recipes.cost: Staff time and the CMMS you already pay for. Nestor is free.[^31]

recipes.name: 2. Five to ten critical machines: open sensors you run
recipes.when: You have a technician or engineer who likes data, and you want to own the data. Simple thresholds often do the job before any model.[^12]
flow: Maintenance manager: choose up to 10 critical rotating machines from recipe 1
Technician: mount sensors and check the mounts monthly
Reliability lead: set simple alarm thresholds first, such as a fixed vibration level that triggers an alert[^12]
Technician: for 90 days, confirm every alert by hand and log it as caught, false or unclear
Maintenance manager: review the alert log monthly and adjust thresholds
recipes.cost: About $4,200 to $5,550 in list-price hardware for 10-12 points, before installation, per our 26 Nov 2026 check.[^7][^8] Software runs from $70 a year (Monnit Premiere) to bring your own (NCD).[^32][^33]

recipes.name: 3. No one reads vibration data: a managed service
recipes.when: No one on staff can read vibration data. On MaintainX already, its Asset Intelligence add-on brings machine data into the CMMS, price on request.[^34]
flow: Maintenance manager: shortlist 2 services and ask for a trial on your own machines; KCF offers a $199, 30-day trial of 48 sensors[^35]
Vendor analyst: sends a diagnosis with each alert
Maintenance manager: tracks confirmed catches and false alarms against the contract
recipes.cost: Mostly quote-only: Tractian, Augury, Waites and Siemens Senseye publish no price.[^36][^30][^37][^38] Petasense's Starter plan lists at $999 a month, billed yearly, as read on 26 Nov 2026.[^39]

rules.name: NFPA 70B, Standard for Electrical Equipment Maintenance
rules.status: Standard since the 2023 edition; binding where adopted
rules.what: Requires a written electrical maintenance program, qualified people and recorded corrective actions.[^14][^26] It sets infrared scan intervals by equipment condition, so monitoring data feeds the schedule.[^25] It binds where your inspector, insurer or contract adopts it.

rules.name: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 (lockout/tagout)
rules.what: An AI alert changes when you service a machine, not how. Lock out and tag out before any repair it triggers.[^15]

rules.name: ISO 17359:2018, condition monitoring guidelines
rules.what: A checklist for a monitoring program: cost-benefit, a criticality review, alert criteria, the decisions that follow and training.[^9][^10]

rules.name: CISA, NSA and FBI: Principles for the Secure Integration of AI in Operational Technology (OT)
rules.what: Be careful with AI that can act on the plant. Keep people in the loop and protect the control network that sensors join.[^49]

rules.name: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3
rules.what: The US reference for securing the plant networks your sensors and gateways connect to.[^50]

howToTest: Pick 5-10 critical machines at one site whose failures are random and costly, using the table above.[^1][^29]
Record 12 months of baseline for those machines: unplanned downtime hours, emergency work orders and actual PM completion. Limble's vendor survey found teams complete 54% of scheduled PM.[^17]
Add a "how was this found" field to every work order: inspection, alert, operator or breakdown. One study found it missing on 60-98% of work orders at four companies.[^6]
Write the alarm rule down before day one, so nobody moves the goalposts.[^9]
Log every alert as caught (confirmed by a technician), false or unclear, with the lead time before failure and the technician hours it took.[^4][^51]
Count avoided downtime only on confirmed catches, at your own cost per downtime hour. Skip survey averages: Siemens' figures come from the world's 500 largest firms.[^52]
Net value is avoided downtime, minus false-alarm visits and needless stops, minus a year of fees. McKinsey saw a 10% false-alarm rate add 1,000 cases a year and erase the savings.[^4]
At day 90, decide per machine: keep it, switch to a simple threshold, or go back to scheduled checks.[^12]
watchOuts: False alarms: in a McKinsey example, a model catching a quarter of breakdowns still lost money when 10% of its alerts were false.[^4][^51] Log every alert, and tune or drop noisy machines.
Dirty work orders: NIST found entry errors are non-random and skew maintenance KPIs, even with large samples.[^5][^53] Clean the history and add a how-found field before you train anything.
No one acts on the alert. DOE warns the savings are "not readily seen by management", so report confirmed catches monthly.[^3]
Sensors bought before a plan. Start from asset criticality: ISO 17359 builds monitoring on a cost-benefit and criticality review, and simple thresholds often do the job.[^9][^12]
Vendor exits: Amazon closed Monitron to new customers in Oct 2024 and shut Lookout for Equipment on 7 Oct 2026.[^40][^54] Ask who owns your data and how you export it.
Over-maintaining: NASA notes scheduled overhauls can raise failure rates by adding early-life failures after the work.[^1] Drop PM tasks that don't match how the part fails.

faq.q: Predictive vs preventive maintenance: which should come first?
faq.a: Preventive for parts that wear with use; condition checks for parts that fail at random, which is most of them in reliability-centred maintenance studies.[^1][^23] DOE puts predictive savings at 8-12% over preventive.[^3]

faq.q: Is predictive maintenance worth it, or mostly a sales pitch?
faq.a: On a few critical machines with costly random failures, often yes; across the whole plant, often no.[^12] A 10% false-positive rate erased the savings in one McKinsey example.[^4]

faq.q: Do we need sensors, or can we start with the data we have?
faq.a: Start with your work orders: find repeat failures and fix the PM.[^18] NIST's free Nestor tool tags free-text work orders.[^31] Then add sensors to the few machines that justify them.[^12]

faq.q: How accurate is our CMMS data, really?
faq.a: Often less than reports suggest: NIST found entry errors hide inside KPIs.[^5] One technician wrote, "Management thinks we're 90% compliant. We're maybe 40%." Clean it before you train any model.[^53]

faq.q: Is a sensor subscription worth it if it saves one or two breakdowns a year?
faq.a: Only if one avoided breakdown costs more than a year of fees plus the false-alarm visits.[^4] Test it on your own downtime cost, not survey averages from much larger firms.[^52]

faq.q: What does a 5-10 machine pilot cost?
faq.a: Our 26 Nov 2026 check found self-run hardware for 10-12 points at about $4,200 to $5,550 list.[^7][^8] KCF offers a $199, 30-day trial, and most managed services publish no price.[^35][^36]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when you have no data team and your machines are standard motors, pumps, fans and gearboxes. Most firms buy: 76% of enterprise AI use cases are bought, per Menlo Ventures.[^55] Internal builds succeed about a third as often as bought or partnered tools, in MIT research on AI pilots.[^56]
buyVsBuild.build: Build only for fleets of identical machines or a process no vendor knows. McKinsey's offshore case took 10-15 data scientists two years and 500+ models.[^19] The middle path: buy open hardware such as NCD or Monnit, keep the data, and start with thresholds.[^33][^12]

pickElse: Parts that wear with use and have a known life: keep time-based PM.[^1][^23]
One narrow, well-known failure mode: a simple threshold alarm in the sensor's own software.[^12][^32]
Low PM completion or a barely used CMMS: fix that first with planned routes in the CMMS you have. Deloitte says get the basics in place before predictive.[^29][^17]
Electrical distribution gear: a scheduled NFPA 70B infrared program before any AI.[^14][^25]

offer.heading: Not sure which machines are worth monitoring? Get a free 30-minute diagnostic
offer.body: Bring your 10 most critical machines and last year's breakdowns. In 30 minutes you leave with which need sensors, which just need better PM, and a before-and-after measure for a 90-day pilot. No sales pitch.

reviews.notes: Wanted durations and the order of moves, not just roles. Recipe 1 now picks the top 10 machines within a month and recipe 2 runs a 90-day alert log. teamAfter trimmed to four bullets (dropped the routes bullet, which repeated the technician role) so each one is a distinct change in the team's week.

Stalled on maintenance jargon: CMMS, PM, RCM, vibration spectra, IO-Link, OT, Condition 3, false-positive rate, thresholds. Each is now spelled out in plain words where it first appears (CMMS as maintenance software, PM as preventive maintenance, Condition 3 as poor condition, threshold as a fixed vibration level that triggers an alert).

Asked whether one site can pilot first, what it does to the unit's margin, and how much technician time it eats. The test now picks 5-10 machines at one site, logs technician hours per alert, and gives a net-value line: avoided downtime minus false-alarm visits, needless stops and a year of fees.

The maintenance manager wanted to know if this lives inside the CMMS they already run, and distrusted kit prices that hide install work. Recipe 3 now names MaintainX's Asset Intelligence add-on (Contact Sales) as the in-CMMS route, and the recipe 2 cost says before installation. Liked that alarm levels, run-or-stop calls and electrical work stay with named roles; no vibration severity numbers added because none were sourced.

Steve could see the question, the hardware price and the first step (clean the work orders) in 10 seconds, and liked that a free start with no sensors comes first. He wanted the next step to say what it is and how long: the offer heading now names the free 30-minute diagnostic. He'd distrust vendor ROI claims, so the Augury 310% stays labelled as vendor-commissioned, and the published-results table says plainly that none comes from a firm his size.

answers.human-role: A technician confirms each alert on the machine, the planner decides when the repair happens, and the maintenance manager signs off run-or-stop calls.[^9][^10][^13]
answers.team-after: Your team moves from firefighting to planned work: alerts give lead time, so the planner books repairs before breakdowns, and technicians write fuller work orders.[^16][^17]
answers.example: An AI maintenance alert names the machine and the fault trend, matches it to past work orders, and suggests a next step a technician must confirm first.[^10] Each alert also carries a confidence level.[^4]
answers.table-1: Use calendar PM for parts that wear out with use, condition checks for parts that fail at random with warning, and run-to-failure for cheap, redundant parts.[^23][^3] Trial AI prediction on critical machines with known failure modes.[^12]
answers.table-2: Published results show predictive saving 8-12% over preventive, and 20-80% less downtime in large-firm cases, but none comes from a 40-500 person plant.[^3][^19][^29]
answers.own-data: Self-run sensors for 10 machines list at about $4,200 to $5,550 in hardware before installation, and most managed services publish no price.[^7][^8][^36]
answers.recipes: Start from work orders if PM is shaky; add open sensors to 5-10 critical machines if someone likes data, or use a managed service if nobody reads vibration data.[^29][^12]
answers.rules: NFPA 70B covers electrical maintenance where adopted, OSHA lockout covers every repair, ISO 17359 guides the monitoring program, and CISA and NIST cover plant-network security.[^14][^15][^9][^49][^50]
answers.benchmark: Pick 5-10 critical machines, record a 12-month baseline, fix the alarm rule before day one, log every alert as caught or false, then decide per machine at day 90.[^17][^9][^4][^12]
answers.what-goes-wrong: Predictive maintenance goes wrong through false alarms, dirty work orders, alerts nobody acts on, sensors without context, vendor exits and over-maintaining.[^4][^5][^40][^1]
answers.something-else: Pick something else when parts wear on a known life, one failure mode needs only a threshold alarm, your CMMS is barely used, or the gear is electrical distribution.[^1][^12][^17][^14]
